analysis.one_liner: Bans PAC money from federal elections, caps out-of-district donations, and ends soft money.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 48 Republican cosponsors but never got a hearing or vote in the House committee that controlled it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten campaign finance law: political action committees — the fundraising arms set up by corporations, trade associations, and labor unions — could no longer give or spend money in federal elections. House candidates could accept no more money from people outside their district than from people who live in it. Unlimited 'soft money' to party committees would have been brought under the rules, lobbyists and PACs could no longer bundle checks for candidates, and incumbents' leadership committees would be banned. It also gave challengers party money to match a big-spending incumbent's war chest and lifted contribution limits against candidates who spend over $100,000 of their own money.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters would see fewer channels for organized money — corporate, trade, and union PACs — to reach federal candidates. Challengers would benefit directly: they could receive party money matching an incumbent's carried-forward war chest, and contribution limits would disappear against rich self-funders. House members who rely on small local donors would compete on closer to even terms, since out-of-district money would be capped at the amount raised in-district.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits PACs from making contributions, soliciting funds, or spending money to influence federal elections, removing corporate, trade-association, and union PAC money from federal campaigns.
Caps House candidates' fundraising from people outside their congressional district at the amount they raise from local residents, with penalties up to five times the excess.

Requires party committees to fund voter drives and mixed political activities only from accounts subject to federal contribution limits and reporting, closing the 'soft money' loophole, and repeals the building-fund exception.
Lets a challenger's party committee contribute unlimited funds to match campaign money an incumbent carries forward from an earlier election.

Bans PACs and registered lobbyists from bundling contributions, bans PAC-to-PAC transfers, and prohibits candidates from maintaining leadership committees or transferring money between principal campaign committees.

Requires corporations, labor organizations, and nonprofits to report any election-related payments not already counted as contributions or expenditures, and lifts contribution limits against candidates whose opponents spend more than $100,000 of personal money.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, trade associations, and labor unions would lose their PAC channels into federal elections. Lobbyists and PACs that bundle contributions would lose that role. Incumbents who raise heavily from out-of-district donors or operate leadership PACs would face new limits, and party committees would lose unlimited soft-money spending.

drawbacks.text: Banning PACs outright can push the same money toward channels the bill did not regulate, such as independent spending; the bill only added disclosure for corporations, unions, and nonprofits, and money that loses one route historically finds another.

The requirement that House candidates raise as much from local residents as from outsiders would penalize candidates whose support crosses district lines, including incumbents who represent their whole state's interests or challengers with statewide or national appeal.

The labor provisions require unions to notify every employee annually about political spending, obtain independent CPA audits of political expense claims, and escrow disputed agency fees during challenges — a substantial compliance burden that unions would bear.
Enforcing a local-resident cap and matching war-chest rules would demand new certification and tracking from every campaign committee and the Federal Election Commission.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The PAC ban, soft-money limits, bundling ban, and disclosure rules are a coherent package for reducing organized-money influence, and the challenger protections counterbalance the incumbent advantages that remain. The weakest part is the local-resident contribution cap, which fights money concentration but also restricts ordinary supporters who happen to live outside the district; the union notice and audit provisions are compliance-heavy but add member transparency. On balance a genuine reform bill, though its one-approach PAC ban might have diverted money rather than removed it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Administration Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Representative Robert Michel, the House Republican leader, introduced the bill on November 8, 1993, joined by 46 original cosponsors including Newt Gingrich, with 48 House Republicans cosponsoring in total.
The bill was referred to the Committee on House Administration the same day it was introduced.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PAC operators and the organizations behind them — corporations, trade associations, and labor unions — kept their legal channel into federal elections. Incumbent members of both parties kept out-of-district fundraising, soft money, and leadership committees, since no reform passed in that Congress.

for.name: Rep. Robert H. Michel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill banning PAC activity in federal elections, with 46 original cosponsors including Newt Gingrich.

for.name: 48 of 435 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican.

against.name: Charlie Rose
against.role: Chair, House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee to which the bill was referred; the committee never held a markup or vote on it, and it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 48 cosponsors were Republicans, reflecting the minority party pushing reform against the Democratic majority; the Democratic-controlled House Administration committee never acted on the bill, so no roll-call was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill bans PAC contributions, solicitation, and spending in federal elections and requires corporations to disclose election-related payments. These entities would lose their principal legal channel for shaping federal campaigns.

Union PAC election activity would be banned, and unions would face annual member notification of political spending, independent audits of political expenses, and escrow requirements for challenged agency fees. Union political money historically flowed heavily to one party, so the ban would fall on a major Democratic funding source along with corporate money.
Registered lobbyists and PACs could no longer act as intermediaries bundling contributions to federal candidates, removing a core service in the influence business.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and their leadership PACs
industries.note: The bill caps out-of-district contributions, lets challengers match incumbents' carried-forward war chests, bans leadership committees and campaign-committee-to-campaign-committee transfers. This is the officeholder class itself bearing the cost of a reform bill.

Party committees would lose unlimited soft-money spending on voter drives and advertising, but would gain the exclusive right to make large matched contributions to challengers facing incumbent war chests.
